Doing it for Yak: Friend's fighting spirit inspires Dolphins duo
Dolphins duo Kurt Donoghoe and Jack Bostock have extra motivation driving them through the club’s historic finals campaign, with the bravery of a close friend inspiring them to make each moment matter.
They pair have seen the unwavering resolve and fight of Jacek 'Yak' McLaurin, whose life was irrevocably changed while playing in a trial match earlier this year for Burleigh Bears. The outside back was involved in a tackle that went tragically wrong, landing on his head.
Kurt Donoghoe has been a key part of the charge to the finals for the Dolphins. ©Scott Davis / NRL Images
He was airlifted to hospital, where it was confirmed he sustained a catastrophic, life-changing spinal injury, where he had no feeling from the shoulders down, including fractures to his C4 and C5 vertebrae.
After undergoing two major surgeries, he is now overseas receiving treatment and provides raw and honest updates on his social media about his progress – and sometimes lack thereof – and the challenges he continues to face.
Speaking before their preliminary final showdown with the Roosters, the pair shared how their friend had helped inspire them all season.
“He inspires me a lot, he definitely motivates me,” Donoghoe told NRL.com.
“What he's gone through, it'd be so hard.
“To see him keep fighting and how strong he's been, it just makes me want to do the same and just keep fighting for success and for greatness.
“I've got another friend that's been in a similar boat, had a bad injury, he would have liked to be playing footy – and I've had a few actually – and just for everyone that has gone down a path like that, it inspires me to just do what I can do because I'm very grateful to be where I am.
“Whenever I play, that's why I try to play every game like it's my last and just try not to ever get too comfortable, because it could all be taken away from me within a minute.”
Jack Bostock has been in fine form for the Dolphins. ©NRL Images
Bostock first met the McLaurin family when he and Jacek were Shellharbour Stingrays juniors together and the friendship has continued ever since.
“It's definitely something I've carried with me for this season,” Bostock said.
“What's happened to him was obviously very, very upsetting for everyone, especially him.
“Going from what he was doing, playing rugby league and doing everything to have that completely taken away from him in a matter of seconds.
“It's pretty upsetting and just to see how strong he is and what he can do, still now for us, he's overseas getting treatment and doing his rehab, but we still catch-up on phone calls every now and then, we chat for hours, and he's so proud of what me and Kurt and also Plathy [Max Plath] are doing at the Dolphins.
“He's met a lot of the boys here through living up here as well, and he's super proud of us, so we just want (to do him proud).

“Especially me, I feel like when I'm going out there, there's definitely a little bit of extra motivation to just know what he would do to get back out on the footy field.
“So just know that every game, play it like it's your last and just give it a red-hot crack for him.
“(His experiences teaches you) every day's not given.”
Since the injury, the rugby league community - like it so often does - has banded together to help raise funds to help support ‘Yak’ and his family.
Friends Kurt Donoghoe, Jacek McLaurin and Jack Bostock in the Dolphins sheds. ©Jacek McLaurin Instagram
There was a Row for Yak challenge and a Sock Round for Yak raising money, while people can also donate directly through the 'Return of the Yak' GoFundMe and Family of League campaign.

Departing Isaako embraces the firsts and lasts in quest for decider
Each step on their journey to finals has been a fresh ‘first’ for the Dolphins, but it has also been the beginning of the end for departing players, including Jamayne Isaako.
A foundation player, Isaako won the club’s inaugural Arthur Beetson Medal as player of year and has never missed a game for the club. And until their Round 19 horror show against the Sharks where they suffered a 66-0 loss, he had scored in every game.
Jamayne Isaako goes for goal. ©NRL Images
However, the bursting stocks of backline talent and rise of young players like Tevita Naufahu meant there was no longer the space to keep him beyond 2026, which he hopes will end with the Dolphins lifting the trophy on grand final day.
He joins Kodi Nikorima (Dragons) and Jake Averillo (Wests Tigers) as players parting ways with the club as season's end, with fan favourite Ray Stone also hanging up his boots.
“Obviously I know I'm leaving at the end of this year and it has been a bit emotional reflecting on it,” the Melbourne-bound Isaako said.
“After the last regular season game against the Titans … driving home on the bus, on the M1, there was a long drive from the Goldie back to Brisbane, but I reflected on it a little bit, and it is a bit of a bittersweet moment.
“I'm moving on at the end of this year, and being in this finals campaign, I want to give it a red-hot crack.
Woolf: 'Back ourselves and enjoy the moment'
“I think everyone understands it's hard to get to this point.
“It's a long season and not too many teams get the opportunity to play finals.
“I'm certainly coming towards the back end of my career and I probably won't have too many of these opportunities again, so it is special to play with the bunch of boys here as well.
“There's so much talent in this group and the sky's the limit for everyone.
“If we can make something work and hopefully get ourselves to the big dance, then I'm sure we'll give ourselves every opportunity to get what we want.”
Jamayne Isaako runs the ball. ©Scott Davis / NRL Images
One of the team’s most reliable performers, the Kiwis winger has also claimed the top-point-scoring award for three of the past four seasons, with his goal-kicking accuracy achieved by following a meticulous routine and putting in countless hours of extras.
“It hasn't been something that I've been thinking of … (but) it's something I’m certainly proud of,” Isaako said.
“Obviously the last couple of years, our attacking – especially here at the Dolphins – has been a credit to scoring a lot of points (to convert with goals).
“Playing on the wing, being a try scoring winger, it's kind of hard to miss (on scoring opportunities) as well.
“So, certainly, proud to have that achievement and three out of the last four years, it's certainly something I'm proud of.”

'Remembers his foundations': DCE ready for full-circle moment
Bob Jones doesn't remember the first time he met Daly Cherry-Evans.
The son of hooker Troy Evans and nephew of Dolphins legends Cam and Steve Cherry, a young Cherry-Evans was always just there.
Whether it was in the locker room after a game or hanging around training during the week, the youngster was a fixture at the club's Redcliffe base during his early years.
DCE excited to return to Redcliffe
"I remember him as a young fella following his dad around," Jones, a club legend and the current Dolphins chairman, said.
"I knew the family very well. The Cherry family had been involved with the club since before my time. Daly's grandfather was a very good player, his uncles were pretty fair players for the club and his cousins were also good players.
"I played one or two games with his dad, as I was finishing up he was coming through."

The Dolphins have progressed to a preliminary final in just their fourth season in the competition and they will have a heaving crowd behind them at Suncorp Stadium on Friday night as they look to book their ticket to the big dance.
Standing in their way are the Roosters, playing in their 13th finals series in the past 14 seasons and chasing the foundation club's 16th premiership.
When the Dolphins entered the NRL in 2023 it was the Roosters they played in their first ever match at Suncorp Stadium and the new boys came away with a 28-18 victory in front of 32,000 fans.
Add on another 18,000 supporters this weekend and The Cauldron will be rocking as Kristian Woolf's men look to take down one of the NRL's superpowers in a mouth-watering do-or-die clash.
The Roosters last tasted premiership success in 2019 with James Tedesco, Daniel Tupou, Victor Radley, Angus Crichton and Nat Butcher all part of the side that downed Canberra 14-8 in the grand final.
On the back of a standout performance in the win over the Sharks, Tedesco will again look to show the way while Crichton will be all the better for the run after playing 30 minutes in his comeback from a foot injury in that match.

'Missing piece': Dynamic hooker changing Roosters premiership fortunes
Roosters hooker Reece Robson has been hailed as the missing piece in the side's quest for their first NRL premiership since 2019.
The unexpected retirement of club legend Jake Friend midway through the 2021 season left the Tricolours with a void at dummy half that they have struggled to feel.
Brandon Smith had two injury-riddled years in 2023 and 2024, and utility Connor Watson has done a serviceable job but the Roosters have largely played without a specialist No.9 until Robson's arrival at the start of this season.
Reece Robson Try
Veteran prop Lindsay Collins said the impact of the hooker's arrival was immediate and backed Robson to lead the Roosters past the Dolphins in Friday's preliminary final.
"He's a player no one really talks about but he's been the missing piece from the last couple of years," Collins told NRL.com. "Not to discredit anyone but our last genuine No.9 was Friendy.
"We haven't had that power game that we were so good at in 18, 19 and 20 since him. Robbo's just come in and it's the small details but as a front rower, the speed of his pass, the crispness of his pass, it hits you on the chest and it gets there quickly.
"Everything starts from him. All our tries on the edges, he has to choose which way the ball goes. He's not just listening, he's seeing as well. He knows where people are moving and the spots to take. He's one of the great minds of this footy era and a bit of an unsung hero in our team, I don't think he gets the credit he deserves."

Relentless, respected, reliable: Nat's a heart and soul Rooster
Forward Nat Butcher is the ‘Quiet Achiever’ of the Sydney Roosters who teammates certainly appreciate even if he gets overlooked at times among the galaxy of stars at the Bondi club.
"He is definitely under-rated - both the Butcher boys are,” Connor Watson told NRL.com of Nat and younger brother Egan.
"To go out for a match and look to your right and see Nat there you just know you're in a good spot."
Butcher is enjoying his 11th season at the Roosters since debuting off the bench as a 19-year-old in the last round of the 2016 season.
He has two premiership rings (2018-19) and made the Junior Kangaroos touring side in 2019 alongside players like Kalyn Ponga, Tino Fa’asuamaleaui and Roosters teammates Angus Crichton and Victor Radley.
Nat Butcher Try
While those four have all gone on to play State of Origin, Butcher’s lone rep jumper came in the 2022 Prime Minister’s XIII.
"He's been doing the same thing since we started playing together and that's just holding down the middle of the field,” Radley said.
"He's someone you want out there because his defence is exceptional - he doesn't miss tackles and he'll have 20 carries.”
Roosters v Sharks - Finals Week 2, 2026
Butcher makes an average 13 carries and 127 metres coming off the bench for the Roosters, with a tackle efficiency of 97.6 per cent. He also has 22 tackle-breaks in his 24 games this year.
"He is Mr Consistent,” Watson said.
"He's had a pretty interrupted last couple of years with injuries (knee reconstruction) and some illness, so for him to get a full pre-season in for us shows because he's been so reliable whether it's off the bench or starting.
Nat Butcher and wife Harmony with son Beau and twins Belle and Billie after a win over the Knights in Round 7. ©Mark Kolbe
"He's played lock, played in the back row and in the front and been consistent in all his performances.”
The 29-year-old Butcher looks almost unflappable on the field with a presence and calmness.
"He is - he has to be - he and Harmony have three kids under three," said Watson.
Son Beau was born in April 2024 and then twin daughters Belle and Billie arrived January this year.
Radley adds: "He's got that spark back this year... he's carrying like Jason Taumalolo.
”He just goes about his work and does it relentlessly.
"This year I feel he's been unbelievable. No matter how much fatigue is in the game if you're looking for someone to get you out of trouble, give you some yardage, it's always him.”

'You can dream': Past pain driving Collins towards GF goal
The chance to finally play in a grand final is driving Lindsay Collins as he looks to lead the Roosters past the Dolphins in Friday night's preliminary final.
Collins featured in the Roosters preliminary final victories in both 2018 and 2019 but was the unlucky man to drop out of the squad for the grand final the following week.
The prop was replaced by Dylan Napa in 2018, who made his return from a three-game ban, with Collins the odd-man out after Cooper Cronk made a miraculous recovery from a fractured shoulder blade. Twelve months later it was Jared Waerea-Hargreaves who was back from suspension for the decider forcing Collins out.
Match Highlights: Roosters v Raiders
A fresh-faced youngster at the time, the prop concedes he figured another shot at a grand final was just around the corner.
Instead it has been seven long years since the Roosters have featured on the first Sunday in October. According to stats compiled by rugby league historian David Middleton, Collins is the only player in the NRL era to have won two preliminary finals but not featured in a grand final.
While he can see the silver linings from the situation, Collins is desperate to lead the Roosters past the Dolphins and into his first decider.
Trent Robinson presented his premiership ring to Lindsay Collins after the 2018 grand final victory.
"The thing is, if they don't get suspended, then I don't even get to experience a preliminary final and I don't get to be part of it," Collins told NRL.com. "I was fortunate to be a part of that because they were out.
"It was my second year in the NRL and I was playing finals and in a prelim. It was the same in '19, it was my third year in the NRL so I was just happy to be there.
"But where I am now in my career, it shows how hard it is to get there and these opportunities don't come by too often. I've learnt from that to make the most of what you have right now.
"Right now we have an opportunity and I've got to make the most of it."

Katoa's quiet confidence grows as Dolphins enter new frontier
A humble son of the Pacific, Isaiya Katoa has had to grow up quickly since taking on the role of halfback and captain at the Dolphins.
Still only 22 years old, he is the youngest captain in the finals series (sharing the duties with forward Tom Gilbert) but has a quiet confidence about himself on and off the field that has grown with each passing season at the club.
From the field: Isaiya Katoa
Since making a ‘surprise’ debut in the maiden game of the club’s inaugural NRL 2023 season as five-eighth under Wayne Bennett, he has since developed into one of the competition’s leading halfbacks.
After taking down the Warriors in their maiden finals match, the Phins are now preparing to take on the Roosters at Suncorp Stadium on Friday night for a place in the decider.
While his actions on the field speak volumes, he is also one of the more eloquent speakers in the game, thoughtful with his responses and respectful of his audience, in line with his Pasifika upbringing.
However, as a young player coming through, he was almost too respectful for his role in the halves, with Dolphins leaders at the time including Jesse Bromwich and Felise Kaufusi telling him to “yell at them” more.
“A lot of credit has to go to my teammates, just allowing me to go out there and demand things and I guess tell them what to do," Katoa said.
“I remember my first couple of years, we had Jesse, Kenny [Bromwich] and Fus, at the time.
Dolphins Isaiya Katoa, Felise Kaufusi and Tom Gilbert make a tackle in their maiden NRL game in season 2023, while Jesse Bromwich looks on. ©Scott Davis / NRL Images
“All three had come from a successful club, all three were some of the best players in their positions at the time.
"I remember they pulled me aside one training session and they said to me, ‘you're the halfback of the team, we want you to tell us what to do, we want you to direct us around, we're not going to get angry at you if you yell at us, that's your job and that's your role as a halfback’ – so that gave me so much confidence in my first couple of years.
“(And) when you pick up that sort of leadership role in being the captain as well, one thing I felt personally was my role didn't really change because as the halfback, you're normally talking anyways and you're normally demanding things.
"(But) I felt the best leaders always lead through their actions and not just through their words, so for me that's always constantly been in the back of my mind and just making sure that if I'm going to lead this team, I lead through my actions rather than my words.
“It's been an awesome learning curve.
“I felt like I haven't gotten everything right and there's still things that I'm always constantly learning, in terms of leadership.
"There's some great leaders at the club here that could also be great captains for this club.
Culture key to Dolphins success
“Tom Gilbert, obviously he's a co-captain with me at the moment and Felise ... he's been a in a leadership role at every club that he's been too, so, for me it’s still a learning curve.
“I know that I've got awesome leaders to lean on if I need advice ... but at the same time as a halfback, I feel like that sort of maturity comes with the position.
"Especially because you've got to be on the ball, you're making probably the most decisions in a game and you normally are driving the mindset of your team as well.”

Dolphins host Sydney Roosters in Finals Week 3 of the 2026 NRL season at Suncorp Stadium on Friday, 25th September. Read on for our full match preview, betting tips, and best odds.
Playing in just the second finals match in club history, the Dolphins are hosting a preliminary final – against a Sydney Roosters team with plentiful big-match experience and newfound momentum.
FORM: The Dolphins are on their second eight-match winning streak of the season, surging to a third-placed finish then producing a gutsy 26-16 win over the Warriors in Auckland on finals debut.
Down 16-8 with 20 minutes left, the Dolphins dominated the last quarter of the match with Herbie Farnworth almost unstoppable as they ran in three tries to stun the heavily-favoured hosts.
The Roosters limped into the finals with three straight losses – and lost halfback Sam Walker to injury – but regained confidence in a gallant 19-12 qualifying final defeat to Penrith where they could easily have prevailed if a couple of things went their way.
They steamrolled an injury-hit Cronulla 46-10 in last week’s semi, scoring five unanswered tries in the second half with Daly Cherry-Evans, Robert Toia and Mark Nawaqanitawase especially prominent.
INS AND OUTS: The Dolphins’ 17 is unchanged, with Felise Kaufusi and Brad Schneider the players rounding out their six-man bench. Tom Flegler has passed concussion protocols after an early exit against the Warriors.
Sam Walker makes a stunning return from the ankle injury he suffered against the Dolphins only four weeks ago, which sees Cherry-Evans go back to five-eighth and Hugo Savala move to the bench.
KEY MATCH-UP: While Isaiya Katoa’s one-on-one battle with Walker will be arguably the most important overall, it’s hard to go past the mouth-watering duel between the NRL’s two form centres, Farnworth and Toia.
HISTORY: The Roosters have a 4-3 edge in the rivalry, but the Dolphins won both clashes this season – a 48-10 rout at Suncorp Stadium with a host of Origin players missing from both teams, and a 26-12 statement win in Sydney in Round 26.
KEY STAT: Mark Nawaqanitawase has scored five tries in three games against the Dolphins.
VERDICT: The Dolphins are looking to join Canberra, St George Illawarra and Wests Tigers as the only clubs in the past 50 years to make a grand final in their maiden finals series.
There’s a sense that the fortnight’s break in this instance could do more harm than good, but Kristian Woolf’s side can take heart from the fact teams with the week off have won 13 of the last 16 preliminary finals.
The Dolphins were outstanding against the Warriors, weathering an hour-long storm to stay within striking distance, then flicking the attacking switch when the opportunities arose in the last 20 minutes. It was a performance that defied their collective lack of playoffs experience.
The Roosters will have taken so much out of their two finals, however, gaining plenty of belief from the high-quality loss to the Panthers then wiping the floor with the Sharks.

The Dolphins have won their last eight at Suncorp Stadium, but the Roosters have a fair record at the ground and are a compelling underdog in what shapes as a down-to-the-wire classic. Expect the 2026 finals trend of low-scorers to continue.

Andrew Johns has warned the Dolphins to be prepared for a fired-up Naufahu Whyte after the Roosters prop was left “screaming” at his coach last week.
The 24-year-old has been the best middle forward in the NRL this year, going past the likes of Payne Haas and James Fisher-Harris for the title.
Naufahu Whyte of the Roosters runs the ball. Getty Images
But as his Chooks pulled Cronulla’s pants down in a 46-10 semi final rout last weekend, the hulking Kiwi was left sitting on the bench by Trent Robinson.
Whyte played just 25 minutes against the Sharks, with Robinson opting to put his best big man on ice ahead of Friday night’s preliminary final clash with the Dolphins at Suncorp Stadium.
Now the Brisbane-based side faces the prospect of a well-rested, and very frustrated Roosters prop tearing them to shreds.
“He wasn’t happy last week, he came out publicly and said,” Johns told Nine’s NRL Tips .
“He only played 25 minutes, he said he was on the bench screaming.

“Which is good, you want him out there.”
While the Roosters beat the Sharks easily to reach the preliminary final, club legend Brad Fittler saw some worrying signs from the Tricolours.
“The one place they looked a little bit vulnerable was when (Sharks hooker) Blayke Brailey went through the middle,” Fittler said.
“Every now and then the Roosters forwards get a little tired and tardy around there, so watch out for (Dolphins hooker) Jeremy Marshall-King.”
The Dolphins have the wood over the Roosters this season, and head into Friday’s game with the added benefit of a week’s rest.
They upset the Warriors in Auckland a fortnight ago to earn that right, and now host a final at Suncorp Stadium for the first time.
Even though the Roosters played last week, Johns pointed out Cronulla didn’t exactly run the Chooks ragged.
“You’ve got to say last week against Cronulla, the last 50 minutes was like a club game,” Johns said.

items.body_excerpt:
He’s been in the NRL for basically five minutes, but Mark Nawaqanitawase has achieved more in his short career than others do over years.
He’s played State of Origin , he’s played for the Kangaroos , and he’s a win away from playing in a grand final .
Mark Nawaqanitawase scores against the Sharks last weekend. Getty Images
Since making the switch from rugby sevens after the Paris 2024 Olympics, ‘Marky Mark’ has undeniably set the NRL on fire. He’s scored tries for fun – and stopped just as many – opposite some of the best wingers in the game, and done it all with a smile.
He scored on debut in the final round of the 2024 season, and virtually hasn’t stopped. He’s scored 43 tries from 45 appearances, including nine doubles, four hat-tricks and even a four-try haul against the Storm in late 2025.
It’s a cliché in sport for a player to say they’re taking it a game at a time, but Nawaqanitawase has been savouring every moment he can with the Roosters before he returns to rugby later this year.
“I’m just happy to be playing another game,” he told media including nine.com.au after the Roosters’ semi final win over the Sharks .
“Obviously, I want to get to the (grand final), but there’s a process to that, and that’s being able to play each week with everyone. It’s exciting to go again.
Read more
Bunnies’ big Latrell call will send centre market into a frenzy
"I've got to try and enjoy every day with a lot of my teammates, with the people at the club."
Nawaqanitawase arrived in the NRL after a four-year stint with the NSW Waratahs , during which time he also played 11 Tests for the Wallabies .
He is returning to the 15-man game with an eye to the home Rugby World Cup next October-November. He is not expecting to play any internationals in either code this year, opting to join his new Japanese club rather than play for Australia at the Rugby League World Cup next month.
But before he leaves, he has one more NRL bucket list item to tick off.
“Just to play for the Roosters was a big thing for me … a huge honour” Nawaqanitawase said.
“Obviously, representing Australia, to don the Blues jersey as well, they’re all great feats. I guess this is another one – going to my first prelim.
Cobbo and Nawaqanitawase leap for a high ball during Origin III. NRL Images
His rivalry with Ronaldo Mulitalo was one of the most fierce in the competition, and he will on Friday night find himself opposite Dolphins flyer Selwyn Cobbo – as he did during Origin.
“He’s having a terrific year, the Dolphins are doing really well … I versed him in Origin, so I know it’s going to be good,” he said.
“It’s going to be a tough effort. He’s a great player, he’s physically a great athlete as well. I will be ready for it.
"Do or die."
The Roosters flew to Brisbane on Thursday ahead of Friday night’s game at Suncorp Stadium.

items.body_excerpt:
The Dolphins are riding one of rugby league's greatest fairytales, chasing a maiden grand final berth in just their fourth campaign, but their next challenge is one they are yet to meet eye to eye.
They have the upper hand against the Roosters in the regular season claiming victory on both occasions they squared off, 48-10 in Round 15 and 26-12 in Round 26.
This regular season success holds more than what meets the eye and there is much more behind the margin of the victories.
Yet being on the receiving end of these results, the Roosters walk into Suncorp on Friday night holding all the cards.
When the sides clashed for the first time this season back in Round 15, the scoreline suggests the Dolphins thrashed the Roosters, which they did, but the credit of this victory is marginal.
The Eastern Suburbs based club were without a host of their Origin stars. James Tedesco , Sam Walker , Lindsay Collins , Reece Robson , Robert Toia , Victor Radley and Mark Nawaqanitawase were all absent on State of Origin duties.
On that night, the Roosters spine read - Cody Ramsey , Hugo Savala , Daly Cherry-Evans and Connor Watson , only one of those a regular first-grade starter week in week out.
SYDNEY, AUSTRALIA - AUGUST 23: Hugo Savala kicking a conversion in the NRL match between Penrith Panthers and Sydney Roosters at CommBank Stadium, on August 23, 2025, in Sydney, Australia. (Photo by Joshua Davis/Zero Digital Sports)
The Dolphins faced a side that was without seven of their key starting players and yes they still had to win the game, which they did, but they were not as heavily impacted by the Origin period.
They were still without five of their regular starters in Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow , Selwyn Cobbo , Tom Flegler , Kulikefu Finefeuiaki and Max Plath , but it was their squad depth that saw them overcome the first challenge the Roosters threw down.
In Round 26 the sides met again. There was no Origin period to compete with, it was two sides charging towards September footy, the Roosters were out to avenge their shock loss to the Tigers the week before, and the Dolphins were shooting for six straight wins.
The The Dolphins won the early battle in Tedesco's first game back after sitting on the sidelines for three weeks with an ankle injury, leading 20-6 at half time.
The Roosters were steadily building momentum to get back into the encounter but that was all undone when Sam Walker went down in the 53rd minute with a syndesmosis injury after getting his ankle caught in a tackle, seemingly ending his season.
The second challenge thrown down by the Roosters was too overcome.
So the record reads, two matches, two Dolphins victories, but that doesn't tell the whole story.
The outfit walking out in the tri-colours on Friday simply have not played the Dolphins .
In their biggest match in their short history, the Redcliffe-based club are now having to face Tedesco, DCE and Walker alongside with a full strength Roosters outfit, the only dent the unknown of Walker's fitness.
SYDNEY, AUSTRALIA - MARCH 17: Sam Walker of the Roosters kicks during the round two NRL match between Manly Sea Eagles and Sydney Roosters at 4 Pines Park, on March 17, 2024, in Sydney, Australia. (Photo by Cameron Spencer/Getty Images)
Seemingly Walker's season was over after getting injured in their last face-off, but now he is back to potentially haunt the Dolphins .
Should the Dolphins and their fans be worried? Short answer is yes, but they have history on their side. They are shooting for their ninth straight victory at their home-away-from-home, a sold-out Suncorp Stadium with a grand final spot on the line.
It is a new challenge for the club, but with their recent form and their newfound ability to not overplay their hand and build pressure, opposed to trying to score on every play, the Dolphins are primed for this contest.

That’s what playing with an injury, or coming back from an injury, is. And the bigger the injury, and the bigger the game, the more intense that psychological warfare with yourself is.

Now, Nathan and the Panthers have been far more vague about their superstar No.7’s “stress-related bone issue” ahead of Sunday’s clash against Newcastle and how he’s travelling, though it seems he’s going to be right to play.
Sam Walker has had a month to heal after surgery on a syndesmosis injury and is closing in on a remarkable recovery to lead the Roosters in Friday’s grand final qualifier against the Dolphins.
Injuries are a fact of life in rugby league, but when they hit, you’re nothing like yourself. You’re filled with self-doubt and even guilt about letting your teammates down. Your routine and training loads are entirely different and for Nathan, I think that’s amplified because he’s the most thorough player I’ve ever seen with his preparation.
Think you can’t target Nathan’s foot injury? Think again
I have a couple of reservations about how Nathan handles this injury, particularly given it’s to his right kicking foot.
The talk is that he will hand the goal kicking over to Dylan Edwards and that Jack Cole (named at five-eighth) or Jack Cogger (who I think could easily start in the halves) will take on more general-play kicking. Either way, it’s not ideal on the left side of the ruck because Cole and Cogger are both right-footers, but obviously not in Nathan’s elite class.
The other issue with ankle and foot injuries is when you’re trying to get up on your toes to sprint and accelerate. This would obviously hamper Cleary’s running game. But I think it could be even more critical to his lateral defensive movements.
One of the few parts of Nathan’s game that can be targeted is that he will occasionally over-chase an attacking side’s lead runners, which we saw most famously in the 2023 grand final against Brisbane when Reece Walsh skewered Penrith.
Defending as the three-man (the third defender in from the sideline) means you have to “double defend” – where you pivot off the opposition’s lead ball-runner or decoy and cover the fullback if they’re sweeping around to the outside.
You need to be able to accelerate, and you certainly don’t need any doubts about whether you can do it.
Especially if it’s Kalyn Ponga, Francis Manuleleua and Bradman Best making a beeline for you.
Manuleleua is just the perfect young back-rower with plenty of mongrel to go after Cleary in this situation. But then again, Liam Martin is the best bodyguard Nathan could ask for, too.
So, does that change the way Penrith defend on their right edge to help out Nathan?
Blaize Talagi was fantastic against the Roosters, but he’s had his issues this year, while Luke Garner and Izack Tago are still there on Ivan Cleary’s extended bench, too.
And don’t worry. Ivan will have a plan to protect his superstar No.7 and the best defensive system in the game, but it’s a fascinating question.
Especially when we’re all wondering how much training he will do , how much movement Penrith can get into Nathan’s foot this week, and how that head noise is playing out between his ears.
